nodes.label: Mandate and the Hashemite Kingdom
nodes.full: What precedes: the invented state, the landlord parliament, the British tie, the oil consortium, the Ottoman-trained officers, the Communist Party and the street risings, and the Development Board. See iraq-1914-1958.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-1914-1958.

nodes.label: Saddam's Iraq
nodes.full: The aftermath: total personal rule, the eight-year war with Iran, the Anfal genocide, the invasion of Kuwait and the Gulf War, the thirteen years of sanctions, and the fall in 2003. See iraq-1979-2003.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-1979-2003.

nodes.label: The Baʿth and pan-Arabism
nodes.full: The party of one Arab nation with an eternal mission — the Syrian and Iraqi wings, the coups, the rivalry with Nasser's Egypt; the ideology and the vehicle of the republican regimes.
nodes.src: background — Adeed Dawisha, 'Arab Nationalism in the Twentieth Century' (2003).

nodes.label: The oil market and OPEC
nodes.full: OPEC, founded in Baghdad in 1960; the consortium's Red Line; the 1973 price shock and embargo — the money that turned a chronically poor state into one of the richest in the region.
nodes.src: background — Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991).

nodes.label: The Cold War and the neighbours
nodes.full: The Soviet Union and its arms, the Shah's Iran and the CIA arming the Kurds, the feud with Baʿthist Syria — and, in 1979, Khomeini's Islamic revolution on the border.
nodes.src: background — Oles Smolansky, 'The USSR and Iraq' (1991); Pierre Razoux, 'The Iran–Iraq War' (2015).

nodes.label: Qasim and the sole leader
nodes.full: Abd al-Karim Qasim, the brigadier who led the 14 July coup, ruled for four and a half years as 'sole leader'. He passed a land reform, left the Baghdad Pact, reclaimed almost all the oil company's concession area, and revived the claim to Kuwait. But he balanced between communists and nationalists until he had no base of his own, and both the Ba'th and the army turned on him.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Juan Romero, 'The Iraqi Revolution of 1958' (2011).

nodes.label: The Ramadan Revolution and the terror of 1963
nodes.full: In February 1963 a Ba'thist–army coup overthrew Qasim, tried him in a night and shot him, and showed his body on television. The Ba'th's paramilitary National Guard then hunted the Communist Party through Baghdad using prepared lists — thousands were killed in a few weeks. The party in power lasted only nine months before the army pushed it out, but the killing had done its work.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Peter Sluglett & Marion Farouk-Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001).

nodes.label: The Arif brothers
nodes.full: Abd al-Salam Arif, a Nasserist officer, took the presidency after ejecting the Ba'th, talked of union with Egypt, and died in a helicopter crash in 1966. His brother Abd al-Rahman held on without direction for two more years — a ceasefire with the Kurds, a lurch toward nationalising the oil, the shock of the 1967 war — until the Ba'th, better organised the second time, came back for good.
nodes.src: Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001); Adeed Dawisha, 'Iraq: A Political History' (2009).

nodes.label: The 1968 coup and the Ba'th consolidation
nodes.full: On 17 July 1968 the Ba'th seized power and this time kept it. Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr was president; the Revolutionary Command Council was the government; the party fused with the state and the army. The first years brought purges, spy trials, public hangings and the building of an intelligence apparatus of several competing services — the machinery of a one-party police state, assembled fast.
nodes.src: Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001); Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989).

nodes.label: Saddam Hussein's rise from the deputy's chair
nodes.full: Officially the deputy chairman of the RCC, Saddam Hussein ran what mattered: the party organisation, the security services, the oil ministry and the Kurdish file. Over eleven years he built a personal machine inside the state and a cult around himself. In July 1979 he pushed al-Bakr out, took the presidency, and — at a filmed party conference — had dozens of 'conspirators' named and led away to be shot.
nodes.src: Con Coughlin, 'Saddam: The Secret Life' (2002); Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party' (2012).

nodes.label: The Iraqi Communist Party
nodes.full: In 1958–59 the Communist Party could put a million people on the streets and was the strongest political force in the country. It was decimated in the 1963 terror, rebuilt, drawn into a hollow 'National Front' with the Ba'th in 1973, and then, from 1978, methodically destroyed — communist officers executed, the party driven underground and into the Kurdish mountains and exile.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978); Tareq Ismael, 'The Rise and Fall of the Communist Party of Iraq' (2008).

nodes.label: The Kurdish movement
nodes.full: Mustafa Barzani came back from Soviet exile in 1958 and by 1961 was at war with Baghdad. The mountain war ran through Qasim, the Arifs and the Ba'th; it produced an autonomy agreement in March 1970 that promised more than any Iraqi government had ever offered the Kurds. The deal collapsed, the war resumed in 1974 with Iranian and American arms — and ended when Iran cut off the supply at Algiers in 1975.
nodes.src: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004); Edmund Ghareeb, 'The Kurdish Question in Iraq' (1981).

nodes.label: The Shia Islamists
nodes.full: As communism and Ba'thism took the Shia young, a religious answer formed at Najaf around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr: the Daʿwa Party, and a body of modern Islamic political and economic thought. The regime read Shia activism as subversion — executing Daʿwa members in 1974, crushing the Karbala procession of 1977 — and by 1979, with revolution across the border in Iran, the confrontation was set.
nodes.src: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003); Rodger Shanahan, 'The Shiʿa of Lebanon' background; Chibli Mallat (1993).

nodes.label: Kirkuk and Mosul, 1959
nodes.full: 1959 was the year the revolution turned on itself. In March a Nasserist-nationalist revolt at Mosul was put down with communist help and days of killing. In July a communist-organised march in Kirkuk exploded into a massacre of the city's Turkmen. Qasim was appalled, blamed the communists, and began to cut them loose — a turn that left him without a shield when the Ba'th came in 1963.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); the Kirkuk events in the ICP and Ba'th accounts.

nodes.label: The killing of the communists
nodes.full: After the February 1963 coup the Ba'th's National Guard ran a campaign of arrest, torture and murder against the Communist Party across Baghdad and the towns, working from lists. The dead numbered in the thousands; the party's leadership and its base among the intelligentsia and the officers were shattered. It was the single most consequential act of violence in republican Iraqi politics.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989).

nodes.label: The First Kurdish War
nodes.full: Barzani's revolt against Qasim in 1961 became a nine-year mountain war fought against three Baghdad governments in turn. Neither side could win: the army held the towns and the roads, the peshmerga held the heights. It ended in March 1970 with an agreement recognising a Kurdish region, a Kurdish vice-president, Kurdish schools and a share of the oil — on paper, the best deal the Kurds ever got.
nodes.src: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004).

nodes.label: The Second Kurdish War and Algiers
nodes.full: When the 1970 deal was not implemented, the war resumed in 1974 — this time with the Shah of Iran and the United States arming the Kurds to bleed Baghdad. In March 1975 Saddam met the Shah at Algiers and traded the Shatt al-Arab border for the end of that support. Iran closed the frontier overnight; the Barzani revolt collapsed in days; and the regime deported hundreds of thousands of Kurds from the border zone.
nodes.src: the Algiers Agreement (6 March 1975); the Pike Committee report on the CIA and the Kurds; David McDowall (2004).

nodes.label: The Arab-Israeli wars and the oil weapon
nodes.full: Iraq sent troops to the 1967 and 1973 wars against Israel, broke relations with the United States after 1967, and used its pipelines as a weapon — cutting the flow to embargoed customers in 1967 and 1973. The wars fed the regime's Arab-nationalist credentials and its hostility to the West, and the 1973 price shock that came with them transformed its finances.
nodes.src: Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007); Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991), on the 1973 embargo.

nodes.label: The 1977 Safar Intifada
nodes.full: In February 1977 the annual walking pilgrimage from Najaf to Karbala turned into an anti-regime demonstration; the security forces fired, and there were arrests, trials and executions. It was the first mass Shia movement against the Ba'th, and the regime's response — and its house arrest of al-Sadr — showed that it now regarded the shrine cities and the Shia clergy as an enemy.
nodes.src: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003).

nodes.label: The land reform and the end of the landlord class
nodes.full: The first act of the republic was a land reform: ceilings on holdings, expropriation of the excess, redistribution to the fallahin, and the abolition of the shaykh's legal powers over 'his' tribesmen. It was imperfectly done — the state could not organise the follow-through — but it broke the few thousand landlord families who had ruled rural Iraq since the Ottoman Land Code, and it was irreversible.
nodes.src: Agrarian Reform Law No. 30 of 1958; Doreen Warriner, 'Land Reform in Principle and Practice' (1969); Hanna Batatu (1978).

nodes.label: The Ba'th and the Revolutionary Command Council
nodes.full: After 1968 the Baʿth was the only legal party, and the Revolutionary Command Council — a handful of party men — was the state. Party and government fused: every ministry, every army unit, every school and union had its party cell and its party watcher. Membership became the road to advancement and the mark of the reliable. It was rule by a self-selecting apparatus, answerable only to itself.
nodes.src: Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party: Inside an Authoritarian Regime' (2012).

nodes.label: The security state
nodes.full: The Baʿth built, in a decade, an apparatus of several competing intelligence services — party intelligence, state security, military intelligence, and Saddam's own units — with informer networks reaching into every workplace and family, purpose-built interrogation centres, and the public hanging as a routine instrument. Fear became the organising principle of Iraqi public life, and stayed so for thirty-five years.
nodes.src: Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear: The Politics of Modern Iraq' (1989); Joseph Sassoon (2012).

nodes.label: The oil nationalisation and the rentier state
nodes.full: Qasim's Law 80 of 1961 reclaimed 99.5 per cent of the concession area; Saddam nationalised the Iraq Petroleum Company outright in June 1972; the 1973 price shock did the rest. A national oil company now ran the country's only real source of wealth, and the state that controlled it controlled everything. The rentier logic — spend without taxing, and answer to no one — was complete.
nodes.src: Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001); Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994).

nodes.label: The welfare state and the developmental Ba'th
nodes.full: For one decade the oil money was spent, in large part, on the people: free education to university, free health care, subsidised food and housing, rural electrification, a mass literacy campaign that won a UNESCO prize, and jobs for women in the state sector. Living standards rose sharply, and a broad urban middle class formed. It is the period Iraqis of a certain age remember with an aching nostalgia.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq: Oil, Wars, Destruction of Development' (1994); Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007).

nodes.label: The Arabisation of the north
nodes.full: To secure the oil districts and the Kurdish border, successive governments and then the Baʿth in earnest deported Kurds and Turkmen from Kirkuk and its region, settled Arab tribes in their place, redrew the provincial boundaries to dilute the Kurdish vote, and stripped tens of thousands of 'Iranian' Iraqis — the Faili Kurds above all — of their citizenship and expelled them. Demographic engineering became state policy.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch, 'Genocide in Iraq: The Anfal Campaign' (1993), on the background; David McDowall (2004).

nodes.label: Ba'thism as the official ideology
nodes.full: The Baʿth taught a doctrine of one Arab nation with an eternal mission, fusing secular Arab nationalism with a loose socialism and a cult first of the party and then of the leader. It was in every school textbook and every official speech and every wall slogan. Few Iraqis believed it; almost all had to perform it. The gap between the loud creed and the private cynicism is one of the marks of the period.
nodes.src: Amatzia Baram, 'Culture, History and Ideology in the Formation of Baʿthist Iraq' (1991).

nodes.label: The Shia Islamic movement rises
nodes.full: Against communism and Baʿthism, a modern Shia Islamism took shape at Najaf around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr — the Daʿwa Party, and a body of political and economic theory meant to answer Marx and the liberals on their own ground. The regime executed Daʿwa members in 1974 and put al-Sadr under house arrest; by 1979, with Khomeini in power next door, it was preparing to move against him for good.
nodes.src: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003); Chibli Mallat, 'The Renewal of Islamic Law: Muhammad Baqer as-Sadr, Najaf and the Shiʿi International' (1993).

nodes.label: The suppression of the secular left
nodes.full: The Communist Party had been the vehicle of a secular, class-based, internationalist politics with a real following among the Shia poor, the minorities and the intelligentsia. Its physical destruction — in 1963 and again from 1978 — closed off that option. What was left in the field were Arab nationalism, which the regime owned, and religion, which it could not. The narrowing of Iraqi political life to those two poles happened here.
nodes.src: Tareq Ismael, 'The Rise and Fall of the Communist Party of Iraq' (2008); Hanna Batatu (1978).

nodes.label: The minorities under the Ba'th
nodes.full: The Baʿth's pluralism was selective. The last Jews were driven out or, in the 1969 spy trials, publicly hanged. Christians were courted — Tariq Aziz, a Chaldean, sat at the top table — as a loyal minority with no external patron. The Yazidis and Mandaeans were tolerated as folklore. The Faili Kurds, Shia and 'of Iranian origin', were expelled by the tens of thousands. Loyalty, not diversity, was the test.
nodes.src: Orit Bashkin, 'New Babylonians' (2012), on the 1969 hangings; Sami Zubaida, 'Contested Nations: Iraq and the Assyrians' (2000).

nodes.label: The poets of the republic and the road to exile
nodes.full: The generation that had made the free-verse revolution — al-Bayati, Saʿdi Yusuf, Buland al-Haidari, and al-Sayyab until his early death — wrote the political poetry of the republic and then, as the censorship tightened and the arrests came, began to leave. Abd al-Wahhab al-Bayati spent most of the period abroad. The Iraqi literary exile that would define the next half-century started here.
nodes.src: Salma Khadra Jayyusi (ed.), 'Modern Arabic Poetry' (1987); Terri DeYoung, 'Placing the Poet' (1998).

nodes.label: Modern Iraqi art under the state
nodes.full: Iraqi modern art stayed strong: Shakir Hassan Al Said's One Dimension Group of 1971 built an abstraction out of the Arabic letter; the sculptors Khaled al-Rahal and Muhammad Ghani Hikmat filled the city with bronze. The state was the great patron — and the censor, and the commissioner of the monuments. Jewad Selim's Monument of Freedom, unveiled in 1961, still presided over the square where the demonstrations gathered.
nodes.src: Nada Shabout, 'Modern Arab Art' (2007); Silvia Naef, 'À la recherche d'une modernité arabe' (1996).

nodes.label: The state claims the ancient past
nodes.full: The republic, and then the Baʿth, made the deep past a national possession: the Sumerians, Hammurabi, Nebuchadnezzar, the Assyrians were now Iraqi ancestors, taught in the schools and stamped on the currency. Iraqi archaeologists took over the digs; the state museum expanded; and the reconstruction of Babylon's walls began — a project Saddam would later make a monument to himself.
nodes.src: Magnus Bernhardsson, 'Reclaiming a Plundered Past' (2005); Amatzia Baram, 'Culture, History and Ideology in the Formation of Baʿthist Iraq' (1991).

nodes.label: The media of the one-party state
nodes.full: The press, radio and television were nationalised and turned into instruments: the party paper al-Thawra, the news read to a fixed script, the president on the screen at the opening of every dam and school. Public life became a matter of the announcement, the parade and the loyalty rally. What real argument survived did so in the coffee-house, the family and the mimeographed leaflet.
nodes.src: Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989); Eric Davis, 'Memories of State' (2005).

nodes.label: The brief flowering of Iraqi cinema and theatre
nodes.full: For a while there was a modernising popular culture: a state film organisation and a handful of serious Iraqi films, the socially pointed theatre of Yusuf al-Ani, a lively television drama, the nightclubs and the record industry, Nazem al-Ghazali's songs. It flourished on the oil money and within the limits of the censor, and the wars of the 1980s onward would close most of it down.
nodes.src: the Iraqi cinema surveys in the Arab film literature; Roger Allen on modern Arab theatre.

nodes.label: al-Sadr and modern Shia political economy
nodes.full: In quick succession Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr published 'Our Philosophy' against materialism, 'Our Economics' against both capitalism and Marxism, and a scheme for interest-free banking. Together they were a systematic Islamic alternative to the ideologies then sweeping the Shia young, worked out in the Najaf seminary. They became the intellectual base of the Daʿwa Party and, later, of the Islamic Republic's economics.
nodes.src: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, 'Falsafatunā' (1959), 'Iqtiṣādunā' (1961), 'al-Bank al-lā-Ribawī fī al-Islām' (1969); Chibli Mallat (1993).

nodes.label: Ba'thist historiography and the invention of tradition
nodes.full: The regime rewrote Iraqi history to suit itself: a continuous Iraqi-Arab identity from Sumer to the 1968 'revolution', the 1920 Revolt as a Baʿthist prophecy, the ancient empires as templates for the present. School textbooks, official festivals and the reconstruction of monuments all served it. History became a department of the propaganda ministry.
nodes.src: Amatzia Baram, 'Culture, History and Ideology in the Formation of Baʿthist Iraq' (1991); Eric Davis, 'Memories of State' (2005).

nodes.label: The developmental social science
nodes.full: The oil-funded developmental state ran on planning: a ministry of planning, the Five-Year Plans, the economists and statisticians and agronomists, the surveys of income and consumption and land. It was a genuine technocratic effort, trained partly abroad, and it produced some of the best data Iraq has ever had on itself — before the wars, the sanctions and the exile of the specialists ended it.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994); Fahim Qubain's earlier survey and its successors.

nodes.label: Ali al-Wardi and the last independent scholarship
nodes.full: The sociologist Ali al-Wardi spent the period writing his six-volume social history of modern Iraq, 'Glimpses of the Social History of Iraq' — the fullest account there is of the Ottoman and mandate centuries, written in a plain, sceptical, sometimes mordant voice. It was independent scholarship of a kind that a tightening police state could barely tolerate, and he was among the last to produce it inside the country.
nodes.src: ʿAli al-Wardi, 'Lamaḥāt Ijtimāʿiyya min Ta'rīkh al-ʿIrāq al-Ḥadīth' (6 vols., 1969–79).

nodes.label: The oil nationalisation and the 1973 boom
nodes.full: Iraq nationalised the Iraq Petroleum Company in June 1972; eighteen months later the 1973 price shock quadrupled the value of every barrel. Oil revenue rose from under a billion dollars a year to more than twenty billion by 1979. A state that had been chronically short of money was suddenly one of the richest in the region, and it spent accordingly.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq: Oil, Wars, Destruction of Development and Prospects, 1950–2010' (1994).

nodes.label: The developmental spending and the welfare boom
nodes.full: The money went into industry — petrochemicals, steel, cement — into roads, dams and power, and into free schooling, free health care, subsidised food and cheap housing. Wages rose, consumption rose, the middle class swelled, and for a few years the improvement was real and broadly shared. It is the material basis of the nostalgia for the 1970s that outlived the regime.
nodes.src: Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001); Abbas Alnasrawi (1994).

nodes.label: The transformation and emptying of the countryside
nodes.full: The land reform broke the estates but the state could not replace them: the cooperatives and state farms mostly failed, the sharecropping system dissolved without a working substitute, and the young kept leaving for the cities where the oil jobs were. Cheap imported food made farming unrewarding. Agriculture's share of the economy collapsed, and rural Iraq — the majority in 1958 — became a minority and a backwater.
nodes.src: Robert Springborg, 'Baʿthism in Practice: Agriculture, Politics and Political Culture in Syria and Iraq' (1981); Abbas Alnasrawi (1994).

nodes.label: The state economy and its distortions
nodes.full: Trade, industry and banking were nationalised in stages; the party controlled the appointments; the plan set the targets. It worked while the oil price was high enough to paper over the inefficiency, the corruption and the growing reliance on imports and foreign contractors for everything from wheat to whole factories. Take the oil price away — as the 1980s would — and the model had nothing underneath it.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994); Kiren Aziz Chaudhry, 'The Price of Wealth' (1997).

nodes.label: The arms economy and the militarisation
nodes.full: A large and rising share of the oil money went to the military: Soviet aircraft, tanks and missiles, French Mirages, and the beginnings of the strategic-weapons programmes — the Osirak nuclear reactor bought from France in 1975, the chemical-weapons plants started at the same time. The guns went in beside the butter through the 1970s, and after 1980 they crowded the butter out.
nodes.src: Anthony Cordesman, 'Iraq and the War of Sanctions' (1999), on the military build-up; the Osirak deal in the IAEA and French sources.

nodes.label: The state oil industry built fast
nodes.full: After nationalisation the Iraq National Oil Company developed the giant North Rumaila field with Soviet help, laid a strategic pipeline linking the northern and southern systems, opened a line to the Turkish coast in 1977, and expanded the refineries and the petrochemical and gas plants. A modern, state-run oil industry was assembled in under a decade — and it was the one thing the regime built that survived every later war.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994); the INOC and IPC company histories.

nodes.label: The dams and the water projects
nodes.full: The republic carried on the taming of the rivers: the Tharthar canal system finished, the Haditha and Mosul dams planned and begun, big drainage schemes to fight the salt that was creeping over the southern fields, and the first work on the Third River — a giant drain to carry saline water off the mid-Euphrates land. Control of the water was now for irrigation and hydropower, not just flood defence.
nodes.src: the Iraqi hydraulic-engineering literature; Peter Beaumont, 'Water and the Middle East' background.

nodes.label: The military and strategic technology
nodes.full: The 1970s brought Iraq a modern arsenal — Soviet MiGs, T-62 tanks, surface-to-air missiles; French Mirages; a ballistic-missile programme — and the start of something more dangerous: the Osirak research reactor and the plutonium ambition, and the chemical-weapons plants at what became the Muthanna complex. The technology base of the wars and the WMD crisis of the next quarter-century was laid in these years.
nodes.src: the reports of the UN Special Commission (UNSCOM) on the origins of the programmes; David Albright, 'Peddling Peril' background.

nodes.label: The infrastructure of the developmental state
nodes.full: By 1979 the modernisation was visible everywhere: the countryside electrified, the telephone and television networks extended, the highways built, the new university city and the expressways and the mass housing in Baghdad. For a moment Iraq looked like a country on a confident upward curve — the physical shell of a modern developed state, put up in twenty years on oil money.
nodes.src: Caecilia Pieri, 'Baghdad: The City in Its Prime' (2015); Abbas Alnasrawi (1994).

nodes.label: Iraq and the Soviet tie
nodes.full: Qasim swung Iraq out of the Western camp and into non-alignment; the Baʿth, needing arms and a shield for the oil nationalisation, signed a Treaty of Friendship with the Soviet Union in 1972 and took Soviet weapons and advisers. Iraq leaned east without becoming a satellite — it kept its oil sales to the West, crushed its own communists, and played Moscow and Paris off against each other.
nodes.src: the Iraqi-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation (April 1972); Oles Smolansky, 'The USSR and Iraq' (1991).

nodes.label: Iraq, OPEC and the oil weapon
nodes.full: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960, and Iraq was among its most hawkish members — first to reclaim its concession area, first among the Gulf states to nationalise its company outright, an advocate of the highest prices and the sharpest use of the embargo. The oil money bought a middle power the means to act well above its weight, and the regime used them.
nodes.src: Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991); Francisco Parra, 'Oil Politics' (2004).

nodes.label: The Kurdish question and the neighbours
nodes.full: The Kurdish war was never only Iraq's. The Shah of Iran and the United States armed the Kurds in 1974 to bleed a hostile Baghdad, and dropped them the moment Iran got what it wanted — the Shatt al-Arab border — at Algiers in 1975. Turkey and Syria watched their own Kurds and interfered as it suited. The Iraqi Kurds learned, at a terrible cost, that they were everyone's instrument and no one's ally.
nodes.src: the Pike Committee report (1976); David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004).

nodes.label: Ba'th against Ba'th — the feud with Syria
nodes.full: After the Baʿth party split in 1966 into an Iraqi and a Syrian wing, the two regimes that both claimed its name became bitter enemies: rival claims to Arab leadership, backing for each other's dissidents, a running quarrel over the sharing of the Euphrates as Syria filled its new dam. A 1978–79 attempt at unity collapsed in mutual accusation. The Arab world's two Baʿthist states could not stand each other.
nodes.src: Eberhard Kienle, 'Baʿth v. Baʿth: The Conflict between Syria and Iraq 1968–1989' (1990).

nodes.label: 1979 — the Iranian Revolution and the alarm in Baghdad
nodes.full: The fall of the Shah and the rise of Khomeini — who had spent fourteen years in exile in Najaf until Saddam expelled him in 1978 — put a revolutionary Shia Islamic republic on Iraq's border, openly calling on Iraq's Shia majority to rise, and encouraging the Daʿwa. For the new president in Baghdad it looked like an existential threat and, with the Iranian army in chaos, an opportunity. The war of 1980 grew directly out of this year.
nodes.src: Efraim Karsh, 'The Iran–Iraq War 1980–1988' (2002); Pierre Razoux, 'The Iran–Iraq War' (2015).

nodes.label: The revolution devours itself
nodes.full: The liberation of 1958 gave way in a decade to coups, mass killings and the police state. Each regime was narrower and more violent than the last — Qasim balancing to nowhere, the 1963 terror, the drifting Arifs, the Baʿth twice — and the country lost, one by one, the checks that a plural politics might have kept: the monarchy, the parliament, the free press, the Communist Party, and finally the army as an autonomous body.
nodes.src: Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

nodes.label: The oil decade
nodes.full: For one stretch — roughly 1973 to 1979 — the oil money was spent, in large part, on the country: schools and hospitals, electrification, a literacy drive, industry, a broad and rising middle class. Iraqis who lived through it remember a modern, confident, secular Baghdad, and remember it with a grief sharpened by everything that came after. It is the great might-have-been of modern Iraq.
nodes.src: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994); the oral-history and memoir literature of 1970s Baghdad.

nodes.label: The making of Saddam's Iraq
nodes.full: The eleven years that al-Bakr was president were the years in which Saddam Hussein, from the deputy's chair, built the thing that would rule Iraq until 2003: the party apparatus, the four rival intelligence services, the Tikriti and clan networks in the key posts, the oil ministry as a personal fief, and the cult. When he took the presidency in July 1979 the machine was already his; the title only formalised it.
nodes.src: Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party' (2012); Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989).

nodes.label: On the edge of the abyss
nodes.full: By the end of 1979 every element of the coming catastrophe was in place: Saddam with absolute power, a revolutionary Shia republic across the border calling to Iraq's majority, the Daʿwa stirring, the Kurds beaten but not gone, a growing arsenal and the beginnings of a WMD programme, and an economy that only worked at a high oil price. The war with Iran was ten months away, and the twenty-four years of ruin had begun.
nodes.src: Pierre Razoux, 'The Iran–Iraq War' (2015); Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007).

nodes.label: Abd al-Karim Qasim
nodes.full: The austere, personally incorruptible brigadier who led the 1958 coup and then ruled alone for four and a half years — passing the land reform, reclaiming the oil concession, claiming Kuwait, and refusing to build a party or a base of his own, trusting instead to a balance between communists and nationalists that in the end protected him from neither. He was tried in a night in February 1963 and shot in a television studio, and his corpse was shown to the country.
nodes.src: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Juan Romero, 'The Iraqi Revolution of 1958' (2011).

nodes.label: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr
nodes.full: The Najaf jurist and philosopher who built a modern Islamic political economy — 'Our Philosophy', 'Our Economics' — and the Daʿwa Party around it, and thereby became the intellectual father of Iraqi Shia Islamism. Put under house arrest by the Baʿth, he was executed with his sister, the writer Bint al-Huda, in April 1980, a few months after Saddam took power. He is the movement's founding martyr.
nodes.src: Chibli Mallat, 'The Renewal of Islamic Law' (1993); Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003).

nodes.label: Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr
nodes.full: The Baʿthist general who was president of Iraq for eleven years — the calm, avuncular public face of a regime whose real power was his younger cousin and deputy. As Saddam's grip closed he was left with the ribbon-cutting; in July 1979 he was eased out with a statement about his health, and in 1982 he died, probably poisoned. He is the figure of the front man outlived by his own creature.
nodes.src: Con Coughlin, 'Saddam: The Secret Life' (2002); Joseph Sassoon (2012).

nodes.label: Mustafa Barzani
nodes.full: The Kurdish leader who fought Baghdad from 1961, won the autonomy agreement of 1970, took arms from the Shah and the CIA in 1974 — and was abandoned overnight when Iran got its border deal at Algiers. He died of cancer in a hospital in the United States in March 1979, in exile, the year the man who had outmanoeuvred him at Algiers became president of Iraq.
nodes.src: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004); Massoud Barzani, 'Mustafa Barzani and the Kurdish Liberation Movement' (2003).

nodes.label: Saddam Hussein, to 1979
nodes.full: A boy from a poor family near Tikrit, a Baʿthist gunman in the 1959 attempt on Qasim's life, a fugitive and then a prisoner, and after 1968 the deputy who quietly took the party, the security services, the oil file and the Kurdish negotiation into his own hands. In July 1979 he took the presidency and, at a party conference he had filmed, read out the names of the men to be led from the hall and shot. The rest of his story is the ruin of Iraq.
nodes.src: Con Coughlin, 'Saddam: The Secret Life' (2002); Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989).
